system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Atomic snapshot
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Wait-free snapshots from single-writer registers via double collects with sequence numbers and helping (embedded scans). Covers direct versus indirect scans, the n+1 collect bound, linearization points, and the bounded-register handshake variant. Excludes the lattice-agreement and LL/SC snapshot algorithms.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C06-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: An atomic snapshot object acts like a collection of $n$ single-writer multi-reader atomic registers, with a special snapshot operation that returns what appears to be the state of all $n$ registers at the same time.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0227-s08] An atomic snapshot object acts like a collection of n single-writer multi-reader atomic registers with a special snapshot operation that returns (what appears to be) the state of all n registers at the same time.
- CS-DIST-C06-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A wait-free atomic snapshot protocol must let any process finish its own snapshot or write even if all the other processes lock up.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0227-s10] But it gets harder if we want a protocol that is wait-free, where any process can ﬁnish its own snapshot or write even if all the others lock up.
- CS-DIST-C06-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A wait-free atomic snapshot protocol must let any process finish its own snapshot or write even if all the other processes lock up, which makes it harder than the failure-free case where the whole register file can simply be locked, read, and unlocked.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0227-s09] This is easy without failures: we simply lock the whole register ﬁle, read them all, and unlock them to let all the starving writers in.
    [CS-DIST-p0227-s10] But it gets harder if we want a protocol that is wait-free, where any process can ﬁnish its own snapshot or write even if all the others lock up.
- CS-DIST-C06-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: A snapshot operation in the helping algorithm terminates after at most n+1 collects, because to avoid the identical-collects case the adversary must supply a new value in every collect after the first, but can supply only one new value for each of the n−1 other processes before some process shows a second new value.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0229-s03] trying to do snapshots all the time, a snapshot operation of a single process is guaranteed to terminate after at most n + 1 collects.
    [CS-DIST-p0229-s04] The reason is that in order to prevent case (a) from holding, the adversary has to supply at least one new value in each collect after the ﬁrst.
    [CS-DIST-p0229-s05] But it can only supply one new value for each of the n −1 processes that aren’t doing collects before case (b) is triggered (it’s triggered by the ﬁrst process that shows up with a second new value).
    [CS-DIST-p0229-s06] Adding up all the collects gives 1 + (n −1) + 1 = n + 1 collects before one of the cases holds.
- CS-DIST-C06-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: If values are tagged with increasing sequence numbers and a process repeats collects (reads of all n registers) until two successive collects return exactly the same vector of values and sequence numbers, then precisely those values were present in the registers at some time between the two collects.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0227-s15] Let’s tag any value written with a sequence number, so that each value written has a seqno ﬁeld attached to it that increases over time.
    [CS-DIST-p0227-s17] Suppose now that we repeatedly perform collects—reads of all n registers—until two successive collects return exactly the same vector of values and sequence numbers.
    [CS-DIST-p0228-s03] values were present in the registers at some time in between the two collects.
- CS-DIST-C06-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: In the Afek et al. algorithm a scan repeats collects until either two successive collects are identical (a direct scan, returning that collect) or it has seen three different sequence numbers from the same process (an indirect scan, returning the snapshot embedded in the second of those writes).
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0228-s10] So a snapshot repeatedly does collects until either (a) it gets two identical collects, in which case it can return the results (a direct scan, or (b) it sees three diﬀerent values from the same process, in which case it can take the snapshot collected by the second write (an indirect scan).
- CS-DIST-C06-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: In the handshake mechanism, a checkHandshake that returns false does not guarantee that the other process did not write its bit, since it may have made a stale write that did not change the value. It guarantees only that the other process did not perform both a read and a write since the checker's previous read.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0231-s24] Then S reads the same value in hD as it read previously.
    [CS-DIST-p0231-s25] This does not necessarily mean that D didn’t write hD during this interval—it is possible that D is just very out of date, and did a write that didn’t change the register value—but it does mean that D didn’t perform both a read and a write since S’s previous read.
- CS-DIST-C06-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The simple scheme of repeating collects until two are identical does not terminate when there are many writers, so writers must be slowed down or made to help by doing snapshots themselves.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0228-s05] Unfortunately, it doesn’t terminate if there are a lot of writers around.1 So we need some way to slow the writers down, or at least get them to do snapshots for us.
- CS-DIST-C06-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The simple repeat-until-two-identical-collects snapshot algorithm does not terminate if there are a lot of writers around, which is why writers must be slowed down or made to help by doing snapshots.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0228-s05] Unfortunately, it doesn’t terminate if there are a lot of writers around.1 So we need some way to slow the writers down, or at least get them to do snapshots for us.
